item.title: NFL news, live updates: Joey Porter Jr. traded to Cowboys; Ravens QB Lamar Jackson limited; Texans WR Nico Collins returns to practice
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news ahead of Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Leading up to Thursday night’s AFC North showdown between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cleveland Browns in Week 4, NFL fans got some blockbuster news Wednesday night.

The Steelers’ stalemate with their star cornerback has officially ended — with a trade, not a contract extension — as news broke that the Steelers are trading CB Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and a conditional 2027 sixth.

On the injury front, Miami Dolphins running back De'Von Achane reportedly suffered a season-ending torn ACL.

Elsewhere, Ravens QB Lamar Jackson was limited in practice on Wednesday with a back issue, though head coach Jesse Minter said it was "something small." The Texans got positive news with star receiver Nico Collins (hamstring) returning to practice, and Rams head coach Sean McVay said he expects WR Puka Nacua (hip) to play this week. Both receivers missed the last two games.

Meanwhile, Vikings WR Justin Jefferson (ankle) and Panthers WR Jalen Coker (quad) and Eagles WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring) all sat out practice Wednesday.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more ahead of Week 4.

item.title: Titans LB Anthony Hill is the defensive rookie of the month
item.description: Dolphins linebacker Jacob Rodriguez is the early betting favorite for defensive rookie of the year, but he wasn't the NFL's choice for defensive rookie of the month.
item.content:encoded:
Dolphins linebacker Jacob Rodriguez is the early betting favorite for defensive rookie of the year, but he wasn't the NFL's choice for defensive rookie of the month.

The NFL announced on Thursday that Titans linebacker Anthony Hill has taken that award. Hill joined the Titans as a second-round pick in April.

Hill leads the entire league with 34 tackles through the first three weeks of the regular season. He has also broken up a pair of passes so far this season.

What Hill has yet to do as a professional is win a game. The Titans are 0-3 and will take on the Ravens as they search for their first victory. If Hill can keep former Titan Derrick Henry under wraps, their chances of obtaining it will look a little better.

Of the four players, Parham’s status was the biggest mystery. Hall’s week to week diagnosis was known, and Mitchell and Taylor were dealing with hand injuries.

After Parham left the Week 3 loss to Detroit with an apparent knee injury, it was easy to fear the worst.

item.title: No. 3 Notre Dame visits North Carolina with a revamped rushing game after NFL departures
item.description: Coach Marcus Freeman views the ground attack as improving.
item.content:encoded:
Notre Dame relied on a pair of NFL-bound running backs last year to nearly reach the College Football Playoff. The third-ranked Fighting Irish have a different-looking ground game for its game at North Carolina.

Notre Dame (4-0) ranks 98th in the Bowl Subdivision in rushing offense at 141.8 yards entering the matchup with the Tar Heels (2-1), with junior Aneyas Williams and sophomore Nolan James Jr. each starting in the backfield so far this year.

Coach Marcus Freeman views that ground attack as improving.

“As long as the guys on the field are producing, we’ll roll them, keep them fresh, try to keep hits off of them,” he said. “But we’re also not going to probably roll them every series just because we want to kind of get them in a rhythm.”

They’ve offered effective play, though it lacks the explosion that came with last year’s duo of Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price. Love was the nation’s No. 5 rusher (114.3) and ran for 18 touchdowns before becoming the third overall pick in the NFL draft. Price ran for 674 yards and 11 scores before going with the last pick of the first round.

With those two leading the way, Notre Dame ranked 17th nationally (203.4) in rushing offense.

Williams started the first three games and leads the Irish in rushing with 224 yards, highlighted by running for 90 yards and two touchdowns in the opener against Wisconsin and then 80 yards with a score against Purdue. Jones broke loose for 121 yards and a score against Michigan State, then started the Purdue game.

“For the two guys we’ve got, the one thing they’ll do is they’ll go north and south,” Freeman said.

Tar Heels aim to connect downfield

North Carolina emerges from an open week trying to figure out how to connect more consistently downfield.

Transfer quarterback Billy Edwards Jr. is coming off a loss at Clemson in which he threw for just 135 yards while completing 13 of 30 passes (43.3%) as the Tar Heels squandered a two-touchdown lead. He completed 57.1% (16 of 28) against TCU in the team’s other game against an FBS foe.

“In the end, it’s team execution,” coach Bill Belichick said. “It doesn’t all come back to one guy, even though everybody wants to focus on the quarterback. There are other things that we need to do better. ... That’s what we’re working on and we’ll keep working on it.”

Irish’s defense will offer a test for UNC

Generating more downfield won’t be easy. Notre Dame’s defense is ranked 11th nationally in scoring (17.6) and 22nd in total defense (313.5).

“Notre Dame’s tough, they haven’t given up many big plays so we’re going to have to execute well to make those happen,” Belichick said. “That’s certainly part of the plan, I’m just saying it’s not easy against them — at least it hasn’t been, they’ve done a good job.”

The frequency of penalty flags will be a factor to watch

Notre Dame and North Carolina have avoided many self-inflicted mistakes.

The Irish are the least-penalized team in FBS play through four games, being whistled for 10 penalties through four games (2.5 average). They also lead the country by averaging just 26.5 yards in penalties per game.

The Tar Heels are close behind. Their 31.7 yards per game is ranked fourth in FBS, while their 13 penalties through three games (4.3) is 11th.

Williams, Freeman move past ‘Lawnmower’ celebration penalty

Williams said that he took one for the team, actually the offensive line, with a celebration penalty in the Michigan State game. Williams said that his offensive line suggested a “Crank the Lawnmower” celebration after his touchdown against the Spartans, though it triggered a penalty.

“They owe me one,” Williams said of his offensive line.

When Williams ran to the Fighting Irish sidelines, he was confronted by Freeman, who looked upset about the penalty. Freeman later apologized to Williams and to his mother for the incident.

“He knows I’m a mama’s boy, so that’s the first person he thought about,” Williams said of Freeman’s apology of his mother. “My mom knows. She can handle it.”

item.title: Vikings KR Myles Price named the NFC special teams player of the month
item.description: Myles Price was named the NFC's special teams player of the week on Wednesday and Thursday brought another award for the Vikings wideout.
item.content:encoded:
Myles Price was named the NFC's special teams player of the week on Wednesday and Thursday brought another award for the Vikings wideout.

Price has also been named the conference's special teams player of the month. Both awards were firsts for the second-year player.

Price's biggest play in September came last Sunday when he returned a punt 86 yards for a touchdown in Minnesota's 23-16 win over the Buccaneers. It was Price's first NFL touchdown and the first kick return for a touchdown of any kind in the league this year.

Price is averaging 21.4 yards per punt return and he also leads the league with 353 kickoff return yards.

item.title: John Lynch on Mike Evans: ‘Mike’s going to make every attempt to try to play’
item.description: 49ers GM John Lynch also provided an update for Nick Bosa
item.content:encoded:
When the San Francisco 49ers lost Mike Evans during their Week 3 win over the Arizona Cardinals, the visible pain Evans was in looked like a player who would be out for longer than seven days.

During a Thursday morning interview on KNBR, Lynch spoke about his star wide receiver’s toughness:

“I will tell you this: Mike Evans, part of the whole package, when I talk to people like Ronde Barber, my old friend who’s stayed really close with the Bucs, once we got him, I think one of the things Ronde said first was, ‘That’s a tough SOB. And I think we’ve already seen that with Mike. You know, he is old school in his mindset, and he doesn’t want to miss.”

Evans missed Wednesday’s session with the rib injury he sustained this past Sunday. Lynch isn’t ready to rule Evans out for Sunday just yet, though:

“And so, we’ll always do what’s right for our player and all that stuff, but Mike’s going to make every attempt to try to play, and we’ll see where that goes. It’s still Thursday, and a couple more days before we kick off. He’s dealing with that, and we’ll see if he can get there by Sunday.”

The 49ers could be down multiple receivers, as Evans wasn’t the only wideout to miss Wednesday’s practice. KhaDarel Hodge was a new addition with a knee injury, which explains Dante Pettis’s signing to the practice squad.

Against the best secondary they’ve faced to date, the 49ers’ wide receivers could consist of: Deebo Samuel, Jacob Cowing, Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks, and Pettis this Sunday.

Not yet for Nick Bosa

The 49ers must’ve felt like Nick Bosa was closer to “week-to-week” since they didn’t place him on Injured Reserve. Bosa pulled his calf muscle in practice last week, missing Week 3.

According to Lynch, it’ll be at least another week until we see the Niners’ best defensive player:

“I think Nick’s doing well. He’s working diligently. I mean, it was just like a week ago today when that happened. And so, he’s worked really hard, and he’ll likely be out this week, and then we’ll go from there. And we’ll look forward to the time when we have Nick back.”

Romello Height was limited on Wednesday. It’d be nice to get him back in the fold, especially if Keion White’s hamstring injury keeps him sidelined. The good news is White was working on the side of the field, so he may be able to contribute in Week 4.

The 49ers aren’t going to rush Bosa back: “But when we bring him back, we’ve got to make sure he’s right on all counts, and he’ll work his tail off until he can get back out there. I think he’s working through it, and when he’s right, we’ll have him back out there. I’m not trying to be vague. Calf injuries are sometimes murky.”

The goal without Bosa doesn’t change: Win more than you lose. A 3-0 cushion helps. Seattle falling in Week 3 did, too. But we know how unpredictable the NFL is, and the Niners could get upset just as easily. Weathering the storm until Bosa returns won’t be easy.

Mykel Williams is likely a week away from returning, but it’s unfair to expect him to look like a first-rounder given the injury he’s coming back from.

item.title: Giants S Jevon Holland named the NFC defensive player of the month
item.description: The Giants wrapped up a 12-7 win over the Titans last Sunday when safety Jevon Holland intercepted a pass in the end zone and the play also wrapped up a stellar month for Holland.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants wrapped up a 12-7 win over the Titans last Sunday when safety Jevon Holland intercepted a pass in the end zone and the play also wrapped up a stellar month for Holland.

Holland had an interception in each of the three games that the Giants played in September, which has already given him a career high for a single season. Holland was also credited with 12 tackles, two forced fumbles and a fumble recovery while helping the team to a 2-1 start to the year.

On Thursday, the NFL recognized Holland's effort by naming him the NFC's defensive player of the month for September.

Holland will try to add to his exploits against the Cardinals this Sunday and the Giants will take all that he can give after losing quarterback Jaxson Dart and linebacker Brian Burns to season-ending knee injuries over the last couple of weeks.

item.title: Brock Purdy is the NFC offensive player of the month
item.description: The 49ers have dealt with a slew of injuries over the first month of the season, but quarterback Brock Purdy has stayed healthy and he's a big reason why the team is 3-0.
item.content:encoded:
The 49ers have dealt with a slew of injuries over the first month of the season, but quarterback Brock Purdy has stayed healthy and he's a big reason why the team is 3-0.

Purdy has gone 60-of-83 for 789 yards, nine touchdowns and an interception so far this season. His nine touchdown passes lead the league and he leads the league in a number of other metrics, including quarterback rating. On top of that, Purdy has not been sacked yet this year.

That production and the 49ers' record made Purdy the NFL's choice for the NFC offensive player of the month for September.

Purdy was also the NFC offensive player of the week in Week 2, but this is the first time that he's taken the monthly prize.

item.title: Kelvin Sheppard defends Detroit Lions’ odd hail mary defense
item.description: The Detroit Lions utilized an odd strategy to defend the hail mary, but defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard defended it.
item.content:encoded:
At the end of the first half of the Detroit Lions’ Week 3 game against the New York Jets, the Jets had eight seconds left to cut into Detroit’s lead.

On the first play, the Lions deployed a common defense, which was to have several defensive backs lined up deep, and another set of players guarding the sideline. Given that the Jets had no timeouts left, the Lions were trying to ensure that any play toward the boundaries would be stopped in bounds, forcing the clock to run out, or defend against a hail mary.

That defense worked, and Jets quarterback Geno Smith couldn’t find an open receiver by the sideline.

That left three seconds left in the half, and the Lions essentially deployed a very similar defense. That raised questions about the strategy, since it doesn’t seem necessary to defend the sidelines anymore, given that a normal play would almost certainly exhaust all three remaining seconds. And by having defenders on the sideline—not in the end zone or not as part of the one-man pass rush—it looks like wasted defenders.

The Jets’ hail mary attempt fell harmlessly incomplete, but it still felt like an unnecessary risk.

On Thursday, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard defended the call, citing a specific situation they were defending against—without revealing what it was.

“We practice hail marys against that defense every week for six years. There’s a couple different ways you play the hail mary. We essentially have two to three different ways we can combat hail marys. The other alternative—my friend that was on the other sideline [Aaron Glenn]—knows it in an out, because we did it here for four years, and he was ready for it. A couple years ago, there was a certain team who exposed that certain defense, and if they would’ve thrown it to a certain player, we all would’ve been sick to our stomach. Luckily, they didn’t. I won’t reveal to the public what I’m talking about, but those that know, know. So I went into that game not only playing the Jets, but playing Aaron Glenn. […] We’ve practiced for six years that exact sideline defense, it converts against the hail mary and we practiced it every week, and I like where we were at.”

It’s not a very specific answer from Sheppard, and it matches coach Dan Campbell similarly vague defense of the play, as well.

“You can do one or the other,” Campbell said about not pass rushing on the hail mary. “And I think for us, let’s stay in it. We went back and forth talking about that last one. If anything, you could go last play and let’s just all defend the goal line. We’re not rushing anyway. I mean time, they’re just going to get back there and then let’s be where we’re supposed to be. We know we’re going up for the ball, cover man, get in front of them. I think it’s a little bit of flavor with where you’re at.”

Regarding the “wasted” players on the sideline, Sheppard refuted that characterization of those players, noting that by the time the hail mary was thrown, those players were near the goal line.

“At the end of the play, you see where they ended up,” Sheppard said.

Upon review, he is right that they were by the ball during the play.

It’s possible that those players are in place to defend the second wave of Jets receivers around the 5-yard line in case of a deflection back toward the field of play, but Sheppard didn’t provide any clarity.

In the end, the Lions are confident they chose the right defense, so don’t be surprised if they play similar situations the exact same way moving forward.

item.title: NFL odds, betting, storylines: 3 underdogs to back in Week 4
item.description: Let's look at three spots where some 'dogs are in position to bark.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes in life, you've got to go against the grain. And in this case, the "grain" is the vast majority of the NFL betting public with my Week 4 NFL underdog recommendations.

Not only am I backing one team that has yet to win a game or cover a point spread, and another team whose quarterback has six more turnovers than touchdown passes, but in both instances I'm fading two squads that are 3-0 SU and ATS.

My third NFL underdog recommendation? Let's ride the only other franchise that — to the shock of most everyone — is off to a 3-0 start on the field and in the wagering department.

Patriots at Bills (-6.5)

The Bills are one of those 3-0 SU and ATS squads. The Patriots, meanwhile, have dropped two of their first three (both on the road), with the latest being an atrocious performance in Jacksonville.

In other words, this is the quintessential sell-high, buy-low situation.

Look, I get it: New England quarterback Drake Maye (one touchdown pass, seven turnovers) has been an unmitigated disaster. At the same time, Buffalo's Josh Allen (five passing touchdowns, six rushing touchdowns) is currently — and deservedly — favored to win his second MVP in three years.

However, contrary to their perfect record, the Bills haven't been perfect in execution. In Week 1, they struggled to put away a Houston team that remains winless. In that contest, the Texans put up 31 points (they have since scored 23 in two games against Cincinnati and Indianapolis).

And while Buffalo led wire-to-wire against Detroit in Week 2, the Lions made things interesting in the second half (while scoring 31 points in the final three quarters). Then last week, following a 10-day layoff, the Bills fell behind 10-0 to a Chargers squad that lost its first two games at home to Arizona and Las Vegas.

Yes, Buffalo overcame that deficit and five turnovers — including two Allen interceptions — to post a comfortable 24-16 victory (thanks in large part to the Chargers being the Chargers). But the point is, the Bills haven't been world-beaters. 

They also didn't have an easy go of it against the Patriots last year, losing 23-20 at home (as 7.5-point favorites) and falling behind 24-7 at New England before rallying for a 35-31 win.

In fact, the Patriots are 5-1 ATS in their last six against Buffalo (all as a 'dog). And last week's ugly showing at Jacksonville aside, New England is still on a 13-4 ATS run (9-2 on the road).

Also of note: The Bills haven't covered the spread in four straight games since early in the 2017 season.

Bet: Patriots +6.5

Dolphins at Vikings (-10.5)

And now for the ultimate sell-high, buy-low scenario: The Miami Dolphins have absolutely lived down to their preseason expectations. Not only are they 0-3 SU and ATS, but all three losses were by 14-plus points.

The Dolphins are tied for dead last (with the aforementioned Patriots) in scoring offense (12 points per game). They're one of five teams allowing more than 28 points per game. And their only real asset — running back De'Von Achane — will be in street clothes the rest of the season after tearing his ACL last week against Kansas City.

Meanwhile, Miami's Week 4 opponent is 3-0 SU and ATS this season after closing out 2025 on a five-game winning streak (4-0-1 ATS).

So why am I quite possibly the only person on the planet willing to invest in the Dolphins this week? The plain and simple answer: This point spread is absurd. Because Minnesota isn't nearly as good as its untarnished record suggests.

Consider these facts: 

The Vikings got outgained 419-239 in their season-opening win over Green Bay (a game the Packers led 22-10 late in the third quarter). 

The Vikings got outgained 297-246 in their 9-3 win at Chicago in Week 2 (a game the Bears were poised to win until Caleb Williams tweaked his hamstring late).

The Vikings got outgained 243-230 (and produced just nine first downs) in last week's 23-16 win at Tampa Bay.

Out of 32 NFL teams, Minnesota ranks 32nd in total offense (238.3 ypg), 32nd in passing offense (137 ypg), 32nd in first downs (39) and 31st in third-down conversion rate.

I know the Vikings' defense has been as dominant as the offense has been inept. But this team has no business being a double-digit favorite. Against anyone. Including Miami.

Bet: Dolphins +10.5

Chiefs (-4.5) at Raiders

I was highly impressed with the Chiefs in their 31-10 season-opening beatdown of Denver. I have not been impressed — at all — since.

In the Week 2 Sunday night contest, the Colts handed Kansas City a 33-30 win, thanks to horrendous coaching decisions in overtime (and the Chiefs failed to cover as 6-point home favorites). 

Then last week, KC went to Miami, outgained the Dolphins by a whopping 5 yards (334-329) and needed 10 fourth-quarter points to turn a 14-10 nail-biter into a 24-10 victory that was far from a work of art.

As for the Raiders, I have been fully impressed — with everything — from the very first snap. And it's not just that they're another team that's 3-0 SU and ATS. It's how Las Vegas has performed across the board.

The offense has been productive (27, 26 and 35 points in victories over the Dolphins, Chargers and Saints) and efficient (only four turnovers). The defense has been stout (18 points, 316.7 yards per game), physical (10 sacks, tied for fourth most in the league) and opportunistic (nine forced turnovers). And perhaps most surprisingly, the Raiders — yes, Raiders — have been disciplined, committing just 17 penalties (tied for fifth fewest in the NFL).

Obviously, this is a huge step up in competition for a team led by 38-year-old quarterback Kirk Cousins (whose 107.2 rating is right behind the 108.9 rating of Patrick Mahomes). But I believe the new-look Silver & Black is ready to meet the challenge.

Do I expect Las Vegas to win? Tough to go there, considering it has beaten Mahomes just twice in 15 tries. But I do expect the Raiders to get inside the number — something they've done in five of their last seven games as an underdog and four of the last five times they've faced the Chiefs.

Bet: Raiders +4.5

LAST WEEK: 2-0

SEASON: 4 -4

item.title: AFC North Preview, Week 4: Steelers and Browns face off in primetime at 2-1
item.description: Previewing every AFC North team’s matchup in Week 4
item.content:encoded:
After three weeks, all four teams in the AFC North have the same record, sitting at 2-1 each. The Steelers, Browns and Ravens were each victorious in Week 2, while the Bengals lost to Pittsburgh in the first divisional contest of the season. Let’s take a look at the updated standings and break down each team’s upcoming matchup in Week 4.

Updated Standings:

  1. Pittsburgh Steelers 2-1
  2. Baltimore Ravens 2-1
  3. Cleveland Browns 2-1
  4. Cincinnati Bengals 2-1
Pittsburgh Steelers

Matchup:@ Cleveland Browns, 8:15pm EST (Thursday Night)

The Steelers are coming off a nail-biting win over the Bengals last week, where they squeezed out a 30-27 victory in a surprisingly high-scoring affair. In doing so, Pittsburgh jumped out to an early 1-0 record in the division, which places them atop the standings despite all teams having the same record. The Steelers had their best offensive performance of the season thus far in Week 3, gaining over 400 total yards with 22 first downs. They’ll look to replicate this success as road favorites against the Browns on Thursday Night Football.

The biggest revelation for the Steelers from last game is they found success on the ground. Without Rico Dowdle (toe) in the lineup, Jaylen Warren totaled 127 rushing yards on just 17 carries — while also adding another 49 yards as a receiver. Expect Warren to be featured heavily again versus Cleveland’s defense, whose front seven has been strong so far this year. Pittsburgh was also able to get complimentary pass-catchers like Roman Wilson and Broderick Washington involved in the passing game. Aaron Rodgers should continue spreading the ball around to keep the Browns’ defense honest.

On the other side of the ball, the Steelers had their worst performance of the early season last week, but there’s reason for optimism in this matchup. While they’ve won their last two games, the Browns still rank bottom-five in both passing yards and rushing yards per game. If the Steelers can get pressure on Deshaun Watson and prevent the Browns from unlocking any explosive plays, they should be able to keep points to a minimum.

Cleveland Browns

Matchup:vs. Pittsburgh Steelers, 8:15pm EST (Thursday Night)

The aforementioned Browns are coming off a second straight win after looking lifeless in the regular season opener. Cleveland narrowly defeated the Carolina Panthers at home, 21-18, and won both recent games by a combined seven points. Nevertheless, the Browns defense has been playing well, and they’re getting more complimentary play on the offensive side of the ball. This week’s divisional matchup against the Steelers at home will be a big test for head coach Todd Monken’s team.

Much has been made about Deshaun Watson’s sudden turnaround and while his play has improved, the Browns’ passing attack has still been limited to mostly short-yardage throws. The biggest factor for Watson is avoiding turnovers, which he’s done much better with no interceptions since Week 1. Watson’s scrambling ability has also been a weapon for the Browns, as he’s rushed for 105 yards overall with a 21-yard run last week. The Steelers will likely try to heat up Watson under center. If the Browns can connect on a couple of explosive plays, that could be a huge lift for them.

On defense, look for the Browns to make a concerted effort to keep Warren contained. If the Steelers struggle to run the ball, they are much less potent offensively. Mason Graham has been a force in the middle of the defensive front with four sacks in three games. He could be big X-factor against Zach Frazier, one of the top centers in the league. The Browns’ defensive backs match up well against Pittsburgh’s pass-catchers on paper, so they may feel comfortable playing a lot of man coverage to cause more havoc at the line of scrimmage.

Baltimore Ravens

Matchup: vs. Tennessee Titans, 1:00pm EST

The Ravens came out of their trip to Brazil as winners of a thrilling game against the Dallas Cowboys. A back-and-forth, high-scoring affair saw the Ravens escape with a 34-31 victory following late-game heroics from Lamar Jackson, Zay Flowers and Tyler Loop, who kicked the game-winning 56-yard field goal. It was far from a perfect win but much-needed, as they staved off another potential blown double-digit lead defeat. Now, the Ravens will look to secure their first win at home this year in a favorable matchup against the Titans.

The Titans rank second-to-last in yards per game and have scored the third fewest points, averaging 12.3 through three weeks. They’ve had two chances to win close games over the past two weeks but came up short, losing by a combined nine points. This is a prime chance for Jesse Minter’s defense to have a breakout performance, which has been up-and-down so far. Expect Minter to dial up blitzes often against second-year quarterback Cam Ward and create exotic defensive looks. The former No. 1 overall pick has thrown for 168 yards per game so far.

Tennessee’s defense has been much more formidable, ranking No. 10 in yards and points allowed per game. The biggest challenge for the Ravens’ offensively will be blocking up front, particularly limiting the damage of All-Pro defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons. The onus will be on Vega Ioane, who is set to start at center for the first time, John Simpson and Andrew Vorhees/Emery Jones Jr. to hold up. The Ravens have been a bottom-tier pass protection team so far this season. Derrick Henry will be facing his former team for the first time since leaving Tennessee, so expect him to be extra motivated to have another productive afternoon.

Cincinnati Bengals

Matchup: vs. Jacksonville Jaguars, 1:00pm EST

As mentioned previously, the Bengals dropped a close game to the Steelers last week on the road, giving them their first loss of the season. They took a big step back defensively in that matchup, allowing over 400 yards and 22 first downs, and will look to bounce back in a difficult Week 4 matchup. The Bengals are hosting a talented Jaguars team that is also 2-1 and has a point differential of +46 this season, which ranks No. 2 narrowly behind the San Francisco 49ers.

In slowing down the Jaguars’ offense, the Bengals will need to key in on Parker Washington, who is an emerging star at wide receiver. Washington has 15 catches for 221 receiving yards and three touchdowns through three games, establishing himself as Trevor Lawrence’s go-to target. The Bengals are allowing 260 passing yards per game, which ranks fifth-worst in the league. Their ability to force turnovers against Lawrence and limit explosive plays will be key for pulling out a win.

On offense, the Bengals will try again to unlock more explosive plays in the run game. Chase Brown’s longest rush of the season so far has gone for only 12 yards. Joe Burrow has started to build some momentum with five touchdowns and no turnovers over the past two games. The Jaguars’ is Top 10 against the run but allows the ninth-most passing yards per game, so this may be another Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins-centric game.

item.title: The Seahawks are getting relentlessly blitzed on offense, but why?
item.description: The Seahawks’ style of offense is ripe for the league-wide trend of defenses blitzing more.
item.content:encoded:
If it feels like the Seattle Seahawks offense has faced a lot of extra pressure, your eyes are not deceiving you.

Through three games, Seahawks opponents have blitzed on 43.4% of pass plays (according to NFL Pro/NextGenStats), good for second-highest rate in the NFL behind the Chicago Bears. It’s probably not a coincidence that the Chicago Bears are first and the Green Bay Packers are fourth, as those teams have already felt the wrath of the Minnesota Vikings and Brian Flores’ blitz-a-palooza. Seattle, meanwhile, has faced two of the top five blitzing defenses in the Washington Commanders and New England Patriots. Even the Arizona Cardinals, who rank near the bottom in blitz rate, blitzed Drew Lock above their season average.

This isn’t anything new for the Seahawks, who faced the third-highest blitz rate last season on their way to winning the Super Bowl. What is different is how they’re getting blitzed, and it’s something of a growing trend across the NFL.

JP Acosta, a wonderful SB Nation alum who now works for CBS Sports, recently penned a fascinating column examining a league-wide trend among defensive coordinators. As more teams shift toward under-center plays (usually with 12 and 13 personnel), DCs are just blitzing the hell out of those looks.

If you digest football online, you’ve probably heard this before: “everyone in the NFL is going under center now,” and it’s true. Across the league, NFL teams are going under center to manufacture their offense at a rate we haven’t seen this decade. According to TruMedia, through Week 3, the under-center rate is 42.0%, the highest the league has seen since 2013. If we want to parse it further, on early downs (first and second down), 2026’s 49.6% under-center rate is also the highest since 2013. Even with the higher under-center frequency, the leaguewide success rate under center (47.4%) is also the highest it’s been in that same time period (2025 is second at 46.9%). Teams are returning to ethical football, leaving behind the shotgun/RPO world we thought we’d get after the iconic Rams-Chiefs shootout of 2018.

But how are defenses countering the return to the under-center game that offenses are throwing at them? Longtime college defensive coordinator Don Brown once said to “solve your problems with aggression,” and NFL defenses have taken note. The leaguewide blitz rate against all under-center passes is 51% through three weeks, the highest the NFL has seen since TruMedia started tracking blitz rate in 2006. Teams are leaning into the aggression to cause chaotic plays, but the reason why is a great illustration of the constant battle for supremacy within the white lines.

The Seahawks are one of only a handful of teams that runs the majority of their offense from under-center, so they are ripe for the counter-blitz revolution. Seattle also runs play-action at the second-highest clip in the NFL, which is another relevant data point:

Opposing defenses are blitzing under-center play action passes at a 52% clip through three games, the highest rate TruMedia has ever tracked.

Over 60 percent of Seattle’s under-center dropbacks have been blitzed. Based on NFL Pro tracking, they were blitzed less than half the time from under-center dropbacks in 2025. What is notable, however, is that offensive coordinator Brian Fleury has yet to establish an under-center pass game without play-action. There have only been two non-PA attempts out of 32 under-center dropbacks, one of which was the tying touchdown to Jaxon Smith-Njigba against the New England Patriots. For comparison, the San Francisco 49ers have 15 non-PA passes out of 30 UC dropbacks. With essentially two games of Drew Lock and only one with Darnold (who didn’t have a single non-PA UC pass against the Washington Commanders), it might be too early to declare any tendencies for Fleury, but it wouldn’t make much sense for a Shanahan disciple to only want to use play-action passing from under center.

None of this is necessarily bad, by the way. It’s a defensive counter to a change in offensive strategies, as is the nature of sport. If there’s good news to glean from these three weeks, it’s the fact that Drew Lock and Sam Darnold have both shredded the blitz (from UC, shotgun, and pistol) to the combined tune of 30/41 for 382 yards, 3 TDs, 0 INTs, and only two sacks taken. Seattle’s EPA/pass against the blitz ranks third in the NFL behind the San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs.

JP’s column did dive into defenses using blitzing to combat the proliferation of outside zone runs, which would definitely be relevant to the Seahawks. The only thing I’ll add is that Seattle is still dealing with one of the highest stacked box rates in the NFL at 32.2%. I don’t have the data for run blitz rate, but the Seahawks run game has performed poorly by EPA/play against stacked boxes, so Seattle is having to deal with a steady diet of loading up to stop the run while sending extra pressure to deal with the heavier personnel, under-center looks.

Regardless of whether it’s under center, shotgun, or pistol, one thing is clear: DCs are blitzing more, full stop.

Across the league, blitz rates are skyrocketing. The 32.3% leaguewide blitz rate is the highest in the NFL since 2010, but it’s not all emotional blitzing after a big play. These are calculated moves, schematic tweaks to force offenses out of their under-center comfort zone and swing the odds back in their favor.

…Well, except the Seahawks, who rank 31st in blitz rate. We’ll see if that changes any time soon once the secondary is healthy again.

item.title: NFL Week 4 Game Preview: Chicago Bears vs. New York Jets
item.description: The Chicago Bears host the New York Jets. @SamHouseholder has the preview.
item.content:encoded:
Coming off a short week, the Chicago Bears will have to decide which backup quarterback they want to start against the New York Jets.

Whoever it is, Tyson Bagent or Case Keenum, they will have a tough act to follow. And a tough defense to play against.

The Jets are 1-2, but are much more competitive than they were a season ago. Their two losses have been by a combined 10 points.

On the other side, the Bears need to prove their victories against the Panthers and Eagles weren’t flukes and the outlier on the young season was the Vikings game in the rain.

Taking care of a team still on its rebuild will go a long way in showing the Bears are indeed not going to regress this year.

Let’s meet the Jets.

New York Jets

SB Nation site:Gang Green Nation

Record: 1-2, second in AFC East

Last week: 31-24 loss to the Detroit Lions

Game day, time, TV: Sunday, noon CT, FOX

Spread: Chicago -3.5

Bears all-time record against: 9-4

Historical meetings: The highest-scoring meeting between these teams was back in 2010, when the teams met the day after Christmas in week 16.

The 10-4 Jets came to Chicago to face the 10-4 Bears.

A 10-0 Chicago lead evaporated in the second quarter as Shonn Greene ran for a 3-yard touchdown, Dwight Lowery picked off Jay Cutler and returned it 20 yards for a touchdown and LaDainian Tomlinson rushed for a 3-yard score.

But the Bears answered back as Cutler scrambled for a 2-yard score himself.

In the third quarter, Cutler hit Johnny Knox for a 40-yard score. It was the first of three third-quarter TDs. Cutler also connected with Devin Hester for a 25-yard TD and Knox again for a 26-yard score.

In the meantime, Mark Sanchez found Santonio Holmes for a 23-yard score, but it wasn’t enough.

The Bears won 38-34.

Last meeting: Week 12 of 2022. Who could forget the matchup of Mike White against Trevor Siemian?

White carved up Matt Eberflus’s defense for 315 passing yards and three TDs. Garrett Wilson scored twice and Elijah Moore scored once. 

Byron Pringle scored Chicago’s only touchdown as they got smoked 31-10 by the Jets.

Injury report: The Jets had nine players on their injury report Wednesday.

Limited participation

  • EDGE Kindgley Enagbare
  • S Minkah Fitzpatrick
  • TE Jeremy Ruckert
  • TE Kenyon Sadiq

Did not participate

  • RB Breece Hall 
  • LB Francisco Mauigoa
  • WR Adonai Mitchell
  • OL Dylan Parham
  • TE Mason Taylor

Offense: The Jets come to Chicago ranked 17th in points and 13th in yards.

Their passing offense ranks 11th and their rushing offense ranks 26th.

Geno Smith (75.5 pct cmp/783 yds./4 TD/0 INT) has recaptured the strong play he showed in Seattle a few years ago. 

He also has a bit more to work with than he did last year in Las Vegas. With Garrett Wilson (21 rec./243 yds./2 TD), rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq (12/143/1) and Adonai Mitchell (9/123/0), they’re able to move the ball and score.

Breece Hall (10 rec./102/0 and 51 car./163 yds./1 TD) plays a big role for their offense as a rusher and checkdown. If he can’t go, Braelon Allen (19 att./61/1) will fill in for him.

Defense: The Jets defense comes in ranked 12th in points allowed and second in yards allowed.

Their passing defense ranks third and their rushing defense ranks seventh.

No. 2 overall draft pick David Bailey (2 sk/12 tkls/3 TFL/1 FF/3 QB hits) is playing up to his draft position. Kingsley Enagbare (2 sk/2 TFL/2 QB hits/1 FF), Demario Davis (22 tkl/1 sk/2 TFL/1 QB hit) and Jamien Sherwood (18 tkl/1 PD/2 TFL) are other statistical leaders on the defense.

In the secondary, Azareye’h Thomas (13 tkl/2 PD/2 TFL), Andre Cisco (16 tkl/2 TFL/1 PD) and Dane Belton (16 tkl/1 PD) are patrolling. 

Key matchups: The Jets can be run on. They’re allowing 4.2 yards per attempt, which ranks 18th. Their offense ranks third in average offensive drive length.

Winning the time of possession and getting them off the field are big keys here. Their passing defense ranks high early in the season, so with a backup QB playing, the Bears will have to pick their spots. And establish the run early.

On defense, slowing down the Jets’ running game will be important. If they can get to Geno Smith, he will make some bad throws and turn it over. But if he’s in rhythm, he’s still a good quarterback. Containing Garrett Wilson and Kenyon Sadiq will be big, too.

Key stats

  • The Jets have yet to have a defensive interception this year.
  • The Jets defense is allowing 4.8 yards per play, which is tied for 29th with the Patriots, 49ers and VIkings.
  • New York blitzes 33.6 percent of the time, 25th in the league. The Bears rank second in blitz percentage after Minnesota.
  • Opposing QBs have a 98.6 rating against the Jets, which ranks 23rd.
  • New York’s third down defense ranks fifth, allowing just 32.3 percent of opponents’ third downs to be converted.

A question to encourage discussion? What will it take for the Bears to get a win this week?

item.description: In trading for former Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr., the Cowboys are taking a leap of faith that Porter will play without a new contract.
item.content:encoded:
In trading for former Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr., the Cowboys are taking a leap of faith that Porter will play without a new contract.

The Cowboys have some protection against the possibility of Porter not playing.

Via Todd Archer of ESPN, the 2027 sixth-round pick is tied to Porter being on the gameday roster for at least two games before that selection goes through.

While the second-round pick in 2028 isn't attached to that caveat, the Cowboys would be in line for a 2028 third-round compensatory pick if Porter leaves as a free agent in March.

If Porter immediately suits up for Sunday's game against the Texans, the term most likely will be satisfied. If, for some reason, the "back" and "conditioning" issues linger, the Cowboys will keep their 2027 sixth-round pick.

item.title: Steelers trade Joey Porter Jr. to Cowboys after offseason contract talks failed
item.description: Pittsburgh traded cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to Dallas for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-rounder after failing to come to terms on a contract extension.
item.content:encoded:
Just last week, Joey Porter Jr. told reporters he “definitely” would play for the Pittsburgh Steelers this season despite a contract standoff and a lingering back issue.

That’s not going to happen. The Steelers have traded the fourth-year cornerback to Dallas for a second-round 2028 draft pick and a sixth-round 2027 pick, the Cowboys announced Thursday morning.

“Here I come...... Dallas,” Porter wrote on a post to his Instagram Stories early Thursday.

Read more:NFL Week 4 picks: Rams defeat Eagles; Chiefs topple Raiders

The son of a former Steelers great — Joey Porter Sr. won a Super Bowl with the Steelers during his 13 years as an NFL linebacker and spent several years with the team as a defensive coach — Porter was selected by Pittsburgh in the second round of the 2023 draft. He broke up 31 passes over his first three seasons.

Porter missed all of training camp and preseason while on the Steelers’ physically unable to perform list because of the reported back issues. During the same period of time, he and the Steelers were unable to come to terms on a contract extension on the rookie deal that was set to expire after this season. The Steelers do not negotiate contracts once a season has begun.

Read more:Rams star Puka Nacua expected to play Sunday; Aaron Donald questionable

Since the season started, Porter has been a limited participant in practices but was inactive in all three games. As the Steelers prepared to face the Cleveland Browns on “Thursday Night Football” this week, Porter was listed as a full participant in practice, although the team added a back injury to Porter’s injury status on Wednesday.

Porter is the third Steelers player traded to the Cowboys in the last two years, following receiver George Pickens last year and offensive lineman Broderick Jones just before this season started. First-year Steelers coach Mike McCarthy was the Cowboys coach from 2020 to 2024.

Last year, a contract dispute led Dallas to deal star edge rusher Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers just before the start of the regular season.

item.description: A quick look at all 16 games for the coming weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Maybe it's good that I'm no longer doing the Joint Mega Picks Podcast.

From 10-6 to 9-7 to 8-8, the trend is not my friend. (For the season, I'm 27-21.)

In Week 3, the best pick was Ravens over Cowboys (especially since the wild-guess score prediction was 34-30). Worst pick: Buccaneers over Vikings. Flew too close to the sun on wings of pastrami pick: Bengals over Steelers, based on the erroneous conclusion that Pittsburgh's find-a-way magic dried up when Mike Tomlin left town.

But each week brings another opportunity to land closer to 16-0 than 0-16. Hopefully, this year's weekly one-game slide won't result in 7-9.

Steelers at Browns (Thursday night)

The Steelers have gone 1-7 in Cleveland since 2018. To make matters worse, the Steelers are 0-9 in Thursday night games against AFC North rivals.

What better way to turn the page on the recent past than to go to Cleveland and find a way to win? Aaron Rodgers will need to get his 42-year-old body ready to go on a short week, and the Steelers will need to play well on both sides of the ball.

Browns coach Todd Monken has plenty of experience against the Steelers, given his time with the Ravens. My brain is screaming "Browns!" but my gut is saying that the Steelers will benefit from coach Mike McCarthy's 16-6 record in short-week games.

Steelers 17, Browns 13.

Colts vs. Commanders at London

The Colts ended a long losing streak, thanks to a Texans team that still can't find a way out of its early-season struggles. The Commanders stunned the defending Super Bowl champions, fueled by the kind of performance from Marcus Mariota that will keep Jayden Daniels on the bench until the 32-year-old former full-time starter cools off. Mariota may have at least one more in the tank.

Commanders 24, Colts 20.

Titans at Ravens

Derrick Henry faces his former team for the first time. He'll make them regret letting him go, if they don't already.

Making that task easier is that the Titans can't get anything going. Coach Robert Saleh's reference to quarterback Cam Ward's sacks-induced PTSD means that the clock in his brain is running out before the walls close in on a given play. That likely won't be cured against the Ravens' defense in Baltimore.

Ravens 30, Titans 17.

Patriots at Bills

Of all the teams in the NFL, none relish the regression of the Patriots more than the Bills. On Sunday, Buffalo could essentially nail down the AFC East and set the table for a run to the No. 1 seed, given their ability to run roughshod against overmatched division rivals.

Bills 34, Patriots 21.

Jets at Bears

Former Lions coordinators get together in Chicago. The Jets are improving, but the Bears have the better team on both sides of the ball — even without their starting quarterback. Or their preferred backup.

Bears 27, Jets 17.

Jaguars at Bengals

Trevor Lawrence has beaten every team in the AFC except the Bengals. Last year, Jake Browning engineered the win after Joe Burrow left with a toe injury. And if, as Burrow believes, the 2026 Bengals have 2019 LSU vibes, a 2-2 start is not acceptable.

Bengals 28, Jaguars 27.

Cowboys at Texans

The battle of Texas takes a back seat to the fact that both teams need this one, badly. Until Houston can muster consistent and effective offense, it's hard to envision them turning it around.

Last year, the Texans became the second team to get to the playoffs after starting 0-3. This year, they may end up having a chance to be the second team to get there after starting 0-4.

Cowboys 27, Texans 20.

Cardinals at Giants

The Giants have a chance to get another win while they further adjust to life without Jaxson Dart. And Jameis Winston needs to start worrying about staving off J.J. McCarthy.

Giants 23, Cardinals 17.

Rams at Eagles

Last year, a wild play on a game-winning field-goal attempt by the Rams gave the Eagles a win. This year, the Rams will make sure to not let it be that close.

Rams 30, Eagles 20.

Packers at Buccaneers

The Bay of Pigs is back. If Green Bay with extra time to prepare can't beat an undrafted rookie quarterback making his first start, they should dissolve the corporation.

Packers 21, Buccaneers 13.

Dolphins at Vikings

This is a candidate for Correction Sunday. But the Dolphins have lost one of their best players for the year (De'Von Achane) and the Vikings' defense is good enough to win games even if the offense adopts a punt-on-first-down strategy.

Vikings 24, Dolphins 14.

Chiefs at Raiders

The NFL is better when the Raiders are good. It's at its best when the Chiefs-Raiders rivalry is relevant.

Chiefs 23, Raiders 16.

Chargers at Seahawks

There's plenty of Harbaugh DNA in this one, literally and figuratively. That won't matter much, because the Seahawks got an unexpected wakeup call against the Commanders.

Seahawks 27, Chargers 13.

Broncos at 49ers

The Shanahan Bowl has high stakes for both teams. While the injuries are piling up (again) in San Francisco, they have enough to hold serve in the latest potential Super Bowl preview.

49ers 24, Broncos 20.

Lions at Panthers

The Panthers have carried over less of the "division champs" vibe and more of the "8-9-for-a-reason" vibe. And the Lions definitely can't afford to lose games they should win.

Lions 31, Panthers 21.

Falcons at Saints

Twenty years after one of the most significant regular-season games in New Orleans history between these two teams, the Saints can't lose to their most despised rivals, can they?

Saints 23, Falcons 17.

item.title: Packers’ offense must go back to square one
item.description: Duo til we die.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers have spent the last couple of years, the seasons with Josh Jacobs on the roster, utilizing a fundamentally different running game than they had in Matt LaFleur’s first few seasons in Green Bay. LaFleur had come from the long-storied Shanahan tree of coaches, and had coached with both father Mike and son Kyle. He was an offensive assistant under Gary Kubiak, a Mike Shanahan disciple, and was Sean McVay’s non-playcalling offensive coordinator in Los Angeles, both of whom had worked together under Mike Shanahan.

What all of these coaches have in common, in the times that LaFleur was there, is that they were extremely heavy users of zone blocking in the run game, particularly outside zone. When LaFleur came to Green Bay, the Packers had been utilizing a very similar running game to what LaFleur had come from for over a decade, with Mike McCarthy overwhelmingly preferring the same zone blocking schemes in the run game. The Packers personnel was a great fit for it, as the front office had spent a decade drafting quicker undersized offensive linemen for McCarthy while Aaron Jones was basically lab-built for the system’s requirements at running back.

And this mostly worked well for a few years. The Packers offensive line deteriorated, primarily because of David Bakhtiari’s horror-show knee issues, but after the 2023 season, the Packers made an active choice to change their structure. We actually saw it started to take shape in 2023, as the Packers started to reduce their usage of outside zone in favor of pin-and-pull tosses, counter, and the like. These plays still ask for athleticism from their linemen but use an entirely different structure to open alleys for ball carriers rather than relying on horizontal displacement creating creases.

An offseason choice before the 2023 season, signing free agent Josh Jacobs and moving on from the aging Aaron Jones, forced the change in system. Jacobs lacks Jones’ natural gliding speed to make the timing of outside zone work, but excelled in the phone booth spaces you have to live in running inside zone, duo, power, and most of the “gap scheme” family. The problem was that the Packers had an outside zone offensive line for a duo running back, and they have spent the past two seasons trying to resolve that issue, with … rather poor results. The signing of Aaron Banks, the drafting of Anthony Belton, and the moving of Sean Rhyan to center all were attempts to get bigger and stronger to be able to move bodies vertically in the running game.

And the Packers’ quarterback had changed in this time as well, and he was different than his predecessor in important ways for how this all marries together. Jordan Love is very good, but he’s also very different from Aaron Rodgers. Rodgers spent his entire Packers career operating out of a heavy outside zone running game. When you pair that with play-action, you typically end up with one of two play structures. The most famous for Packers fans would be those deep half-boots, where Rodgers would sometimes end up ten yards behind his offensive line to uncork a deep ball to, most commonly, Jordy Nelson. But the most common is the stereotypical bootleg action, which effectively works as a rollout, and is often accompanied by concepts that look relatively similar to flood, usually with some sort of slide or flat option as the quick check if the edge doesn’t buy the run-action.

Running these types of actions regularly requires a pretty agile quarterback and a pretty quick arm action, both things Rodgers had in spades. Love on the other hand, has a bit of a longer delivery, a necessity given his longer arms, but he is also not as agile as Rodgers was. He has the silly body, after all. Now, Love still can run these actions, and has. It’s just not what Green Bay has gone to as much during his time under center.

The play-action builds off of gap scheme are more befitting to Love’s game. The run-action is more vertical, giving Love a more traditional dropback structure, and also allowing him to target the entirety of the field rather than cutting it down by two-thirds. This has been particularly important for him when targeting digs, crossers, and short posts, where he has thrived. These actions ask less of Love’s agility, but more of his ability to layer throws with velocity, something he excels at.

The reason I bring the play-action up is that the Packers have been stuck between two offenses all season, because the offensive line, the running backs, and the quarterback don’t line up. The offensive line is apocalyptic and has been undersized. Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton, and Jacob Monk are all, ideally, centers. Jennings apparently can’t snap, and Sean Rhyan is playing center so he’s blocking both Burton and Monk there (if Monk is an NFL player at all). The interior group has been legitimately expansion Houston Texans-level bad, but the Packers have at least taken significant steps to fix that problem in the past week, adding veterans Laken Tomlinson, Mekhi Becton, and, most importantly, former Wisconsin Badger Kevin Zietler.

What is noteworthy about these three, particularly Tomlinson and Becton, but even Zeitler at his advanced age, is that they do not fit what Green Bay was trying to run during pre-season, which was a lot of outside zone. These players are here to get vertical displacement in the running game. In the coming weeks, expect to see plenty of duo, plenty of inside zone, plenty of power, etc. And with that, you can build a play-action game that mimics the run looks and a play-action game that plays into the strengths of the quarterback.

Now, there are two massive open questions remaining. Most importantly, are these guys going to be good enough to get the Packers offensive line out of terrible to just below average? They’ll still be starting Anthony Belton, someone who should have been playing guard from the moment he was drafted, at right tackle. Zeitler, who was good last year, had off-season quad surgery, hence why he did not sign until the end of September. Becton alternates between good and terrible depending on the year. And Tomlinson was solidly below-average last year in Houston after a few mediocre years in New York. The last season of his that you could classify as good was the same year Aaron Rodgers won his final MVP. Even getting this line to just normal bad from the expansion-level atrocity they are right now will be a massive upgrade, and the veteran know-how of this group should hopefully improve upon the mess of missed assignments and bad technique in both the run and pass game the line has shown in the first three games.

The second massive question is the running backs. Marshawn Lloyd has been the worst back in the NFL. I’m not talking in EPA or success rate (he’s second-worst in EPA-per-rush and 13th-worst in success rate), I’m talking about having eyes that can see things happening on my screen. Lloyd is dead last in the NFL in rushing yards over expected, and it’s no secret as to why. He’s, by NFL running back standards, blind.

This concern is not new, as it was very prevalent at USC. He was terrible on zone runs, which ask more of his vision, and he was good on gap scheme runs, which largely pre-determine which hole to hit. Even with the scheme change, the Packers should consider finding a different player to take his roster spot, whether that is waiting for the seemingly inevitable Josh Jacobs return at some point, or cutting bait now and finding someone off a practice squad who can at least give you replacement level running back performance.

Lloyd’s primary partner, Kaleb Johnson, has been just as bad. Johnson’s RYOE per attempt is even worse than Lloyd’s, costing the Packers nearly two yards per carry! His EPA is better, simply because of Lloyd’s lost fumble and because the Packers recovered his own, but his success rate is just as porous. And Johnson’s primary issue is the same: he can’t read his blocks. Neither Lloyd nor Johnson have any capacity to run outside zone, which asks more of a running backs ability to read the moving morass than any other play-type. Even if the Packers keep giving carries to both of them, moving to a primarily gap-scheme run game, which more or less tells them exactly where to go, should help both hopefully go from the worst running back duo in the history of the franchise to just normal bad.

And this is all just taking us back to where we’ve been the last two years. A gap scheme run game behind an increasingly big offensive line (the Packers will be approximately the fifth-heaviest offensive line once Zeitler is up to speed and either Banks or Tomlinson man left guard), partnered with a more vertical play-action passing game that can appear the same to the defensive front seven. And hopefully that size and vertical displacement allows the running backs to play on easy mode and just hit the designated spots, and creates a virtuous cycle where the running game can be just good enough to make the play-action passing game a bigger threat.

And this better work. If it doesn’t, everyone might be getting fired.

We're on to Week 4 of the fantasy season! As we look for every advantage this season, the X-factor position is the FLEX. To break it all down, analyst Joel Smyth goes through eight players in the consensus rankings flex zone for your flexes, double flexes or even third WR slots.​

Set & Forget

Josh Downs vs. WAS

So far this season, when Alec Pierce is off the field, Downs has been targeted on 32% of 66 routes. Washington has been poor against wideouts, to say the least. To put things in perspective, the Cardinals have allowed 34 fantasy PPG to WRs, which ranks 31st among defenses.

The Commanders have allowed 39 per game.

Surprisingly, Washington's run defense has improved this season, forcing offenses into heavy passing volume in the first few weeks. The Colts are going to stay run-focused, but when they do throw, it's going to Downs. 

Bhayshul Tuten vs. CIN

The trust in Tuten is growing and the numbers are looking great. This offense is built around the outside run game, where Tuten ranks first among RBs in outside (D Gap) runs, although he's 16th in total carries. That should benefit him against a Cincinnati defense that is overwhelmingly improved after trading the 10th overall pick for DT Dexter Lawrence. The goal-line trends all benefit the Jaguars running back, while a potential receiving uptick could bring him to another level.

After what we've seen in the last three games, Tuten has a shot to be a great fantasy RB2 the rest of the way.

all summer, Liam Coen talked about success rate and creating yards after contact at the RB spot

despite seeing the worst yards before contact per att (0.5) in the league

Bhayshul Tuten through three games:
2nd in success rate
3rd in missed tackles forced per attempt
3rd in the… pic.twitter.com/9cqwSNcgEb

— Josh Norris (@JoshNorris) September 30, 2026

Flex Starts

Michael Wilson vs. NYG

Last season, after averaging 25 receiving yards per game, Wilson suddenly had 18 targets, 15 receptions and 185 receiving yards versus the San Francisco 49ers. Crazy fluke game!

Until it wasn't.

The very next week, with way too many people adding him but not starting him, Wilson had 15 targets, 10 receptions and 118 yards. I don't want that mistake to happen again after a 17-target day versus, coincidentally, the 49ers. He is now fourth in targets behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Chris Olave — AKA, the top-three players in receiving fantasy points. Wilson is the WR5 since that Week 11 breakout last year, and not enough has changed since that point to make me sit him here. 

Braelon Allen vs. CHI

The first backup RB to command heavy waiver attention this season is Braelon Allen, coming to save your roster. I believe Isaiah Davis will get his fair share of work here, but he's had 0% of the RB touches this season, with Allen handling 27%. Allen has two things going for him: one, the Jets offense in 2026 doesn't look like it did in 2025 or before, ranking 16th in scoring offense and 16th in RB fantasy points in the first month. Two, Chicago's run defense has been sub-par, allowing the fourth-most yards per carry. Allen can sub into the starting lineup immediately. 

Double-Flex Starts

Jameson Williams vs. CAR 

It's been a slow start, to say the least. After looking into Williams in depth this week, I was surprised how little has changed since last season. Sam LaPorta's presence is felt, but William is still top-10 in routes, a near-identical role, and it's still the same offensive core in Detroit.

A lot of the little things have added up to make the very boom-bust receiver just a bust receiver: a reception that ended less than a yard away from the end zone, a big drop on a potential 50+ yard catch and more. The Panthers give Williams a great shot of bouncing back with their top-two corners, Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, placed on IR ahead of Sunday Night Football. 

Jacory Croskey-Merritt vs. IND

Indianapolis has struggled against the ground game early and looks to be Croskey-Merritt's easiest matchup yet. The volume has been solid, definitely enough for a second flex position, and his scoring would've looked much better if his 50-yard TD in Week 3 wasn't called back due to an illegal shift. It's a risk with the lack of receiving he provides, yet just good enough to slide into starting lineups in deeper leagues.

Booby Traps

Emeka Egbuka vs. GB

Sadly, Egbuka looks to be continuing his production from the second half of the 2025 season rather than the first half. With Baker Mayfield out Sunday, Tampa Bay will turn to undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels to step up to the plate. In college, Daniels only averaged 6.8 yards per dropback, which would only be middle of the road if he replicated the same numbers versus NFL defenses. Plus, I wouldn't expect many dropbacks in the first place. It's going to take a lot for Egbuka to be what he was at the beginning of the season, which was already a middle-of-the-road flex play. 

Emeka Egbuka has scored 12+ PPR points in one of his last 15 games. pic.twitter.com/2QolZ1txYY

— Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) September 30, 2026

Ollie Gordon II vs. MIN

The Vikings defense has been dominant to start the season under Brian Flores, ranking second in first downs allowed per game with 15. Meanwhile, the Dolphins offense averages 15 first downs per game themselves, ranking 30th. So, the Vikings have made their opponents (GB, CHI, TB) look like the Dolphins offense. What will they make the Dolphins offense look like?

It's scary, to say the least, and Gordon may be splitting work with Jaylen Wright if he returns to play on Sunday.

item.title: NFL Thursday Night Football preview: Suddenly hot Browns with Deshaun Watson take on Steelers
item.description: The Browns and Steelers are both 2-1, coming off Week 3 wins.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns lost 34-10 to the Jacksonville Jaguars in their opener. There was a question if Deshaun Watson would get benched before Week 2. It seemed likely that if he got another start he'd still be replaced by Week 3, which was Cleveland's home opener.

That has changed.

The Browns have won two games in a row. They had late rallies to beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on the road and the Carolina Panthers last week. Watson hasn't been great, but he has been a little better than his first few disastrous seasons with the Browns, and there's no longer daily conversation over whether he'll get benched. This week the Browns go for a three-game winning streak on Thursday night against the Pittsburgh Steelers, who are also off to a 2-1 start and tied for first place in the AFC North. All four teams in the division are 2-1.

The Steelers had a huge win last week, beating the Bengals 30-27. An offense that had scored only one touchdown through two games came alive. Aaron Rodgers had 292 yards passing, and Jaylen Warren had 127 yards rushing. Warren will be in for another big workload this week with Rico Dowdle ruled out due to a toe injury.

For the Browns, the offensive resurgence has been incremental. Watson has 238 and 144 yards in Cleveland's last two games, but that has been enough to help the team to wins. There is a good young core around the quarterback position that is emerging and contributing each of the past two weeks. After the first game of the season it seemed impossible that the Browns might spend any days all alone in first place of the division, but that's where they'll be with a win on Thursday night.

The rivalry between the Browns and Steelers goes back decades and runs deep. This time there are some considerable early-season stakes.

Who needs it more?

It's a dead heat. Both teams are 2-1. Both have questions about their long-term viability as contenders in the AFC North due to their uneven offenses. Perhaps the Browns get the slight edge because it's a home game and if they lose, it will be tough to find road wins in the division to even it out. But these two teams should be pretty pleased to be 2-1, and one of them is going to be 3-1 and in sole possession of first place in the AFC North for a few days.

Key player: Browns RB Quinshon Judkins

The Browns are 2-1, and one would assume that means they've run the ball well. Actually, Cleveland has been one of the worst teams in the NFL on the ground. They Browns are 29th in rushing yards, 29th in rushing yards per attempt and have zero rushing touchdowns. They're 31st in EPA (expected points added) per rush. Judkins, in his second season, has just 124 yards and is averaging 3 yards per attempt. Last season he was averaging 3.6 per attempt before dislocating his ankle and fracturing his fibula. Perhaps that leg injury is still lingering. With Deshaun Watson not producing many yards in the air, the Browns need the running game to emerge to have a consistent offense. Judkins is the key to that. He has 42 rushing attempts this season and no other running back has more than four. Judkins has to start producing for the Browns offense to stay afloat.

Betting market watch, by Ben Fawkes

We probably won't be telling our grandkids about this game, but it remains an important game in the AFC North. The Steelers opened as 2.5-point road favorites, and the line has moved to Pittsburgh -3 at several sportsbooks. The total is a low one at 38.5, up slightly from the opener. This will be the eighth straight game that Cleveland has been an underdog and the 12th time in its last 13 games, dating back to last season. Aaron Rodgers and Pittsburgh's offense looked downright functional last week against Cincinnati, while Deshaun Watson did enough to lead the Browns past Carolina late on Sunday. Cleveland's defense (17th in EPA/play) hasn't been as strong as it has been in previous seasons. I'd look to the over in this game, even as ugly as it feels to take.

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines, by Scott Pianowski

Expectations have to be somewhat muted as the Steelers and Browns kick off Week 4, as the 38.5 total is the lowest of the week. Here are three fantasy themes to consider as you watch the game.

1. Is Harold Fannin Jr. the first read in the Cleveland passing game? Fannin had a quiet opener, but he’s posted a 12-105-2 line since, taking advantage of 15 targets. He was able to overcome the messy QB play in Cleveland last year, and Deshaun Watson’s play the last two weeks has been encouraging.

2. Will the Jaylen Warren show continue? Warren finished as the RB8 last week, given the backfield to himself with Rico Dowdle unavailable. Dowdle won’t play here, which means Warren can push for 20 or more touches against a Cleveland run defense that’s been ordinary (4.5 YPC allowed).

3. Can Quinshon Judkins find room to run? Judkins has seen a touch increase every week, but he’s still struggling to find any space to operate (3.0 YPC). Cleveland’s offensive line is one of the worst in football, but at least it’s up against a Pittsburgh front seven that’s been merely average.
